title: Commission provides guidance to Google for AI interoperability on Android and sharing of Google Search data under the Digital Markets Act
key_claim: Two July 2026 Commission decisions specify that AI chatbots offering search functionalities are eligible to receive Google's shared search data, and that rival AI assistants get Android access equivalent to Google's own, which the Commission says matters to 60% of EU users who have an Android device.
frame_summary: The Commission presents the decisions as a way to let rival AI services compete on equal footing with Google's own AI on Android and in search, treating AI assistants as competitors to Google's services.
verbatim_quote: For example, it specifies that AI chatbots offering search functionalities are eligible to receive shared data, and that, subject to anonymisation, Google should share the same data that it collects to optimise its own search services.
verbatim_list: Third-party AI assistants are therefore limited in how they can offer their innovative services, making them less attractive to 60% of EU users who have an Android device.

title: Commission fines Google for breaches of the Digital Markets Act (press release IP/26/1670)
key_claim: On 23 July 2026 the Commission fined Google EUR460 million for self-preferencing on Search and EUR430 million for Play steering restrictions, set a 60-day compliance clock, and said dialogue continues on applying the decision to AI Overviews and AI Mode.
frame_summary: The Commission frames the fines as the first enforcement of self-preferencing and steering rules, while signalling that the same principles will be tested against Google's AI search features.
verbatim_quote: In this regard, the Commission issued Google a fine of €460 million and a fine of €430 million respectively.
verbatim_list: The Commission also takes note of Google's proposals on how it plans to apply the principles of the decision to AI Overviews and AI Mode, on which dialogue will continue in light of today's decision.
Google is required to comply with the Commission's decisions within 60 days, otherwise it risks periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of its total worldwide turnover.

title: CMA strengthens proposals allowing people choice over their search service
key_claim: On 23 September 2026 the CMA proposed that Google's search choice screens admit AI assistants that meet technical and security criteria, consulted to 9 October, and expects a final decision by the end of the year.
frame_summary: The CMA argues that people increasingly use AI assistants as their search service, so a choice-screen remedy that leaves them out no longer serves users.
verbatim_quote: We've listened carefully to feedback and are responding quickly to the rise of AI assistants, which people are increasingly using as their search service, but aren't included on Google's choice screens.
verbatim_list: Allow AI assistants to be included where they meet the relevant criteria, including technical and security requirements
The CMA is inviting views on its updated proposals by 9 October before reaching a final decision on this conduct requirement which it expects to make by the end of the year.

title: Artificial-intelligence competition in Europe: the role of DMA Article 6(7) (Working Paper 17/2026, Fiona M. Scott Morton)
key_claim: The Commission's Article 6(7) Android specification, issued in draft in April 2026, is a substantive and well-targeted intervention whose aim is that the merits of an AI service, not ownership of a distribution channel, decide commercial success.
frame_summary: Scott Morton argues that opening Android's access points to rival assistants is a well-targeted way to make AI competition turn on product merit instead of distribution control.
verbatim_quote: The merits of an AI service, rather than whether it already owns a distribution channel, will determine its commercial success.
verbatim_list: The European Commission's first Digital Markets Act Article 6(7) specification, issued in draft form in April 2026, is a substantive and well-targeted intervention.

title: CSA research note: EU DMA Android AI interoperability order
key_claim: The Android order turns highly sensitive device capabilities into a standing interoperability surface that any qualifying third-party AI assistant can request equal access to, which the note treats as a security risk.
frame_summary: The Cloud Security Alliance argues that the Android order trades a single vetted integration for a shared access surface whose security certification regime is still undefined.

title: DMA specification decisions on Google
date_evidence: By Rob Bratby | Posted on 17 July 2026 | Updated 4 August 2026
key_claim: An AI chatbot that provides search-engine functionality in the EEA can qualify as a search-data beneficiary if it clears a genuine-economic-activity test; search data sharing starts from January 2027, eleven Android features open by 1 August 2027 at the latest, and data pricing is fixed for five years.
frame_summary: Bratby reads the decisions as a detailed eligibility-and-pricing mechanism that treats AI chatbots as direct beneficiaries alongside conventional search engines.

title: Search choice screen: who qualifies
date_evidence: By Rob Bratby Posted on 24 September 2026
key_claim: Under the CMA's revised proposal an AI assistant qualifies if a significant proportion of its UK users consider it a general search service; the earlier test requiring general search as a core and central part of the service is removed, and listing is only possible in theory.
frame_summary: Bratby sets out the eligibility tests as drafting detail that will decide in practice whether any AI assistant is listed.

title: Google challenges EU orders to open up to AI, search engine rivals
date_evidence: Published: September 29, 2026 | BRUSSELS, Sept 29 (Reuters) - By Foo Yun Chee
key_claim: Google filed challenges on 29 September 2026 to the two July EU orders, saying they share private search history without sufficient anonymisation and weaken Android security; DuckDuckGo calls the appeal a delay tactic and the changes start next year.
frame_summary: Reuters reports the first legal test of the AI-access orders, with Google arguing privacy and security and rivals arguing the appeal only buys time.
verbatim_quote: We're appealing decisions that will force us to share people's private search history without sufficient anonymisation and weaken vital security protections on Android.
verbatim_list: The only thing an appeal buys Google is time.
The changes will kick in next year.
